newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany says Russia refused to amnesty deserters.
newsitem.headline: Germany says Russia refused to amnesty deserters.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Wednesday Russia had refused to grant an amnesty to 600 soldiers who deserted from the former Soviet Army in east Germany, but he believed Moscow would understand if Germany let them stay.

His comments came as Germany conceded for the first time that its intelligence services had questioned most of the deserters -- a fact which the soldiers say means they would certainly be imprisoned as traitors if they were sent home.

"Russia's military prosecutors didn't want to waive the right to prosecute so as not to endanger discipline among the troops," Kinkel told the daily Hamburger Morgenpost in an interview released ahead of publication on Thursday.
"I believe Russia will understand the coalition's decision," said the minister, who discussed the matter with officials in Moscow earlier this month.

Bonn's ruling coalition parties decided in principle on Tuesday that the soldiers, who seized the opportunity to defect after East Germany became a part of the united Germany in 1990, should be allowed to stay. A final decision rests with the interior ministers of the 16 federal states.
Of a total of 1,659 soldiers and family members, only 168 have so far received asylum or residence permits.

Reports that many of the others faced imminent deportation prompted protests from human rights groups and the German soldiers' association who said the men were being discarded because they had outlived their usefulness.
Russian law prescribes a sentence of up to 10 years for desertion and up to 20 years for treason.

In a report to parliament's interior affairs committee on Wednesday, Interior Ministry State Secretary Eduard Lintner said 100 deserters had been questioned by the BND federal intelligence service and 430 by the anti-extremist Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
Kinkel said that despite Moscow's objections, it was only right that the men should be allowed to stay.
"These are people who got caught up between the millstones of global politics in central and eastern Europe during the upheavals of the early 1990s," Kinkel said.
"We can't just treat them like the flotsam and jetsam of the East-West confrontation which we are glad to have overcome."

Most of the soldiers are from Russia, which ran the 340,000-strong Soviet garrison in east Germany after the collapse of the Soviet Union until it completed its pullout in 1994. Some are from Ukraine and other former Soviet republics.

The soldiers say it was not only German intelligence officers who interrogated them at the Federal Office for Asylum Applications in Nuremberg as they were applying for political asylum, but also U.S. and British officials.
A government spokesman, asked about reports that Germany had reprieved the soldiers under pressure from its allies, said he was not aware of this.
Lintner told the interior affairs committee that if allied intelligence services carried out any interviews of the deserters, this was "not known" to Bonn.
